## TL;DR

The outage came from a cleanup promise that treated `ESRCH` as a normal race but rethrew `EPERM`. Because the process-level rejection handler considered every unhandled rejection fatal, one failed signal could terminate the control-plane process. Process-group cleanup now contains both expected signal failures, process-level handling keeps known signal and transient network errors recoverable, and fatal exits leave a durable marker that the next boot surfaces in the dashboard attention feed. The managed service path already requests restart-on-failure from its OS supervisor. The incident note records the root cause and the limit of that guarantee for a foreground server.

## Work and rationale

I started by reading the task’s worktree copy and searching the server, core, and command code for signal calls and process-level handlers. The historical system log mentioned in the task was not present in this worktree, so I followed the source paths directly. The most relevant promise-returning cleanup path was `terminateProcessGroupAndWait` in `src/core/process-group.ts`. It sends SIGTERM and possibly SIGKILL to a detached child group. Its signal helper ignored `ESRCH`, which covers a process group disappearing between its liveness probe and signal, but rethrew all other failures. That made `EPERM` escape an async cleanup function.

I updated the helper to treat `EPERM` and `ESRCH` as an unavailable target. It logs the group leader PID and signal, then resolves. This preserves the cleanup caller’s ability to settle its own run state without promoting an operating-system permission race into an unhandled rejection. Unexpected codes still throw, because silently hiding unrelated programming or OS failures would make cleanup behavior hard to diagnose. A focused test injects both error codes and verifies the cleanup function resolves and logs the target PID.

The existing process-level handler already logs fatal errors with structured details and exits for non-test processes. I kept that behavior for uncaught exceptions and unknown rejection types, but added a narrow classifier for common process signal errors and transient socket/network failures. Such unhandled rejections are logged at error level and do not call `process.exit`; this addresses cleanup and transient transport failures without converting arbitrary logic errors into recoverable conditions. The test suite now exercises the classifier with the relevant codes and a representative unknown error.

For a genuinely fatal exit, I added a best-effort marker under the repository’s configured cache directory. The handler logs the fatal record first, then writes the timestamp and short error summary to the marker. On the next `startServer`, startup reads the marker, records a durable `serverCrash` attention event with the message “Server restarted after a crash,” and removes the marker. The event flows through the existing attention store and dashboard feed, so it survives the restart and does not depend on the previous process’s memory. If writing the marker fails, the fatal system log remains the source of truth.

The task also asked for a supervisor restart. The service manager’s existing generated unit already configures restart-on-failure for installed managed services, so I did not add another competing launcher. I documented the boundary: a foreground server launched directly still relies on whoever launched it to supervise it. The next-boot notice is server-owned and works whenever the server is restarted, including by the managed service supervisor.

Finally, I added the incident summary to `docs/agent-debugging-and-incidents.md`. It records the observed timing context, the error-classification gap, the contained cleanup behavior, and the supervisor limitation so future investigations do not assume that every server invocation is automatically supervised.

## Approaches tried

I searched for direct `process.kill`, `child.kill`, process-group wrappers, global rejection handlers, and the service manager’s restart policy. The task’s named log path was absent in this checkout, so I used code-path evidence rather than claiming to have read the original stack trace. `signalProcessGroup` already swallowed failures for short best-effort signals, but `terminateProcessGroupAndWait` had its own stricter signaling path and was the promise escape point worth hardening. I kept the change there so a teardown routine that promises to wait cannot accidentally continue polling forever after authority has been refused.

I considered a general restart loop in the server process, but that would require an outer process to survive the server it is meant to restart and would duplicate the installed service manager. The existing managed-service restart policy is the right owner for that case. The code change instead makes the restart visible on the next boot through the attention feed.

## Challenges and blockers

The task points to `.repoos/logs/system.log` at a specific timestamp, but that log is not included in this worktree. As a result, the exact original caller and task identifier cannot be proven from the incident trace here. The process-group path is a strong source-level match for a rejected cleanup signal and is covered directly. The process-group helper does not receive a task ID, so its diagnostic identifies the group leader PID and signal; the caller retains responsibility for associating the failed run with its task-level outcome.

The required `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` passed. Remote validation first skipped two hosts after link-throughput probes failed, then ran the full local gate; the scoped build, tests, rendered contrast audit, and UI smoke all passed. I fixed a formatting failure from the first pass with `bun run fmt` before rerunning the check. The remote retry later completed successfully as well.

## Key learnings

Best-effort cleanup has to distinguish “could not signal” from “cleanup logic failed.” `ESRCH` and `EPERM` both mean the caller cannot usefully proceed with a signal, although for different reasons, so neither should escape as a process-wide rejection. A global rejection handler also needs a deliberate error boundary: known transient classes can be logged and contained, while unknown failures should retain fatal behavior until they are understood. Finally, restart behavior belongs to the component that actually outlives the server. The managed service manager can restart a failed child; the child can only leave evidence for the next process, which is what the durable dashboard notice does.
